source_text: Expositio sane, quam Pauli apostoli sermonibus admovisti, cum risu esset praetereunda, nisi Scripturarum terreret ignaros. Cum essetis, inquit Apostolus, servi peccati, liberi fuistis iustitiae [n284] . Dicere utique non poterat: Liberatos; quoniam hic sermo liberationis tunc decenter infertur et proprie, cum homo a noxiis liberatur; liberi autem a virtutibus dici possunt, qui decernunt nihil debere virtutibus. Liber ergo et a bono et a malo dici potest, qui alteri serviens, alteri studet nihil debere; liberatus autem nisi a malo dici non potest; quia verbum hoc liberationis in se habet indicium illius qui propulsatur angoris. Quae igitur hic quaestio Apostolo de verbis suis fieri potuit, cum ille more generis humani, a bono liberos, a malo dixerit liberatos? Cum ergo, inquit, servi essetis peccati, liberi fuistis iustitiae; quem fructum habuistis tunc in his, in quibus nunc erubescitis? [n285] Sed ne tu aestimares servos nos peccato fieri per naturam, audi ipsum Apostolum in iisdem locis loquentem: An nescitis, quoniam cui exhibetis vosmetipsos servos ad oboediendum, servi estis eius cui oboeditis, sive peccati, sive obauditionis iustitiae? [n286] Vosmetipsos, inquit, exhibuistis peccato servos; ut intellegeres eum voluntati, non nativitati imputare peccatum. Ob hoc ergo solum eos dixit liberos fuisse iustitiae, quia detrectassent eius praecepta servare.
pass_a_gloss: The exposition indeed, which you moved up to the speeches of the apostle Paul, would have to be passed by with a laugh, unless it were terrifying those ignorant of the Scriptures. When you were, says the Apostle, slaves of sin, you were free of justice. He could at any rate not say: Freed; since this speech of liberation is then decently brought in and properly, when a human is freed from noxious things; but they can be said free from virtues, who decree that they ought to owe nothing to virtues. Free therefore both from good and from evil can he be said, who serving the one, studies to owe nothing to the other; but freed cannot be said except from evil; because this word of liberation has in itself an indication of that distress which is driven back. What question therefore could here be made to the Apostle about his own words, when he by the custom of the human race said free from good, freed from evil? When therefore, he says, you were slaves of sin, you were free of justice; what fruit did you then have in these, in which now you blush? But lest you estimate that we are made slaves to sin through nature, hear the Apostle himself speaking in the same places: Or do you not know, that to whom you exhibit yourselves slaves unto obeying, you are slaves of him whom you obey, whether of sin, or of the hearing-obedience of justice? You yourselves, he says, exhibited yourselves slaves to sin; that you might understand him to impute sin to will, not to nativity. On account of this therefore alone he said they had been free of justice, because they had declined to keep its precepts.

pass_b_english: Your explanation of the apostle Paul's words would deserve to be passed over with a laugh if it did not frighten those unfamiliar with Scripture. The apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Romans 6:20). He certainly could not have said “freed”. The language of liberation is fittingly and properly used when a person is freed from harmful things. Those who resolve to owe nothing to the virtues, however, can be called free from virtues. A person can therefore be called free either from good or from evil when, serving one, he aims to owe nothing to the other. But a person can be called freed only from evil, because the word “liberation” contains a sign of the distress that is driven away. What difficulty, then, could be raised here about the apostle's words when, following ordinary human usage, he called them free from good and freed from evil?

He says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Romans 6:20–21). But lest you suppose that we become slaves of sin through nature, hear the apostle himself speaking in the same passage: “Do you not know that when you present yourselves as slaves to obey someone, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin or of obedience to righteousness?” (Romans 6:16). He says that you presented yourselves as slaves to sin, so that you would understand him to impute sin to will, not birth. He therefore called them free from righteousness solely because they had refused to keep its commands.
